guide.title: Greenpoint, Brooklyn: Where the Monitor Was Built
guide.intro: European mariners named this East River peninsula for the grassy bluff on its bank. The Dutch bought the land from the Keskachauge in 1638 and called the township Boswijck, and in 1645 the Dutch authorities granted a large tract here to a ship's carpenter, Dirck Volckertsen, known as the Norman, who built his house near what is now Calyer Street, west of Franklin Street. For almost two centuries the peninsula was farmland and stayed isolated from the rest of the region; at the time of the Revolutionary War only five families lived here. That ended in 1832, when Neziah Bliss and Eliphalet Nott bought thirty acres of farmland. Bliss had it surveyed into streets in 1834, and the first road followed in 1838. Industry and immigrants arrived immediately afterward, and Greenpoint has been rebuilding on top of them ever since.

sections.heading: Shipyards, refineries, and the five black arts
sections.body:
Neziah Bliss, born in Hebron, Connecticut, was a steamboat builder and iron-works owner, and he built the connections his thirty acres needed. In 1838 he paid to erect a bridge over Bushwick Creek to the growing village of Williamsburgh, and in 1839 he backed the turnpike along what is now Franklin Street that linked Greenpoint to Williamsburgh and Astoria. The first road in Greenpoint was built in 1838, and industrialization and an influx of residents followed quickly.

What followed was shipbuilding and the five "black" arts: printing, glassmaking, pottery making, oil refining, and cast-iron manufacturing. By 1875 more than 50 oil refineries covered Greenpoint, Williamsburg, and Bushwick. Immigrants from Ireland, England, Russia, Italy, and particularly Poland arrived in large numbers during the late 1800s to work in the factories.

The ironclad USS Monitor was built at the Continental Iron Works here and outfitted at the Brooklyn Navy Yard. Antonio de Filippo's 1939 monument in Msgr. McGolrick Park commemorates the Monitor's 1862 battle with the Merrimac.

Newtown Creek, the industrial waterway bounding the neighborhood, carried the traffic. By 1915 it was one of the busiest waterways in the country: more than 100,000 ships passed through it that year alone, carrying over 5 billion tons of cargo. Then it stopped. Manufacturing and shipbuilding declined through the early 1900s, and by the end of World War II trucks and planes had largely replaced waterborne transport.

What the factories left behind is now protected. The Greenpoint Historic District — 43 acres and 363 buildings dating from 1850 to 1900 — was designated by the Landmarks Preservation Commission on September 14, 1982 and listed on the National Register on September 26, 1983. The Eberhard Faber Pencil Company Historic District on West Street followed on October 30, 2007.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Greenpoint has two subway stations, both on the G and both inside the neighborhood. Greenpoint Avenue sits at the intersection of Greenpoint and Manhattan Avenues. Nassau Avenue sits at Nassau Avenue and Manhattan Avenue, and was the original terminal of the IND Crosstown Line when it opened in 1933. The line was extended toward Downtown Brooklyn in 1937.

NYC Ferry's East River route calls at the Greenpoint landing, at 10 India Street. The route page indicates the Greenpoint landing is served by the East River route's B branch during weekday peak hours and on non-winter weekends rather than by every sailing, so check the current schedule before relying on it.

There is no Long Island Rail Road station in Greenpoint.

sections.heading: Where to stay
sections.body: The research behind this guide could not confirm a currently operating hotel inside Greenpoint. The nearest verified options are in Williamsburg, to the south: the Wythe Hotel at 80 Wythe Avenue, in a converted 1901 brick industrial building, and The William Vale at 111 N 12th St.

faq.question: How do I get to Greenpoint?
faq.answer: The G stops twice in the neighborhood, at Greenpoint Avenue (Greenpoint and Manhattan Avenues) and at Nassau Avenue (Nassau Avenue and Manhattan Avenue). NYC Ferry's East River route also calls at the Greenpoint landing, 10 India Street.

faq.question: Where does the name Greenpoint come from?
faq.answer: European mariners called the peninsula Greenpoint because of a grassy bluff on the bank of the East River. The Dutch bought the land from the Keskachauge people in 1638 and named the township Boswijck.

faq.question: What was the USS Monitor's connection to Greenpoint?
faq.answer: The ironclad was built at the Continental Iron Works in Greenpoint and outfitted at the Brooklyn Navy Yard. Antonio de Filippo's 1939 sculpture in Msgr. McGolrick Park commemorates its 1862 battle with the Merrimac.

faq.question: Which parts of Greenpoint are landmarked?
faq.answer: Two districts. The Greenpoint Historic District, roughly bounded by Kent, Calyer, Noble and Franklin Streets, Clifford Place and Manhattan Avenue, was designated in 1982. The Eberhard Faber Pencil Company Historic District, on West Street between Greenpoint Avenue and Kent Street, was designated in 2007.

faq.question: Why is Msgr. McGolrick Park not called Winthrop Park anymore?
faq.answer: The City of Brooklyn acquired the land in 1889 and named it Winthrop Park for Assemblyman Winthrop Jones. It was renamed in 1941 for Monsignor Edward J. McGolrick, longtime pastor of St. Cecilia's Roman Catholic Church on Herbert Street.

faq.question: Is there a hotel in Greenpoint?
faq.answer: No currently operating hotel inside Greenpoint could be verified for this guide. The nearest verified lodging is in Williamsburg — the Wythe Hotel at 80 Wythe Avenue and The William Vale at 111 N 12th St.

places.name: McCarren Park
places.address: Nassau Ave., Bayard, Leonard & N 12 Sts., Brooklyn
places.summary: A 35-acre park that NYC Parks describes as shared by Greenpoint and Williamsburg, with ballfields, tennis and basketball courts, a running track, and the McCarren Park Pool and Play Center. It was formerly known as Greenpoint Park.
places.history: The park opened in 1906 as Greenpoint Park and was renamed in 1909 for State Senator Patrick H. McCarren. Its WPA-era pool, designed by Aymar Embury II under Robert Moses, opened in 1936, closed after the 1983 season, and sat unused for nearly three decades before a $50 million reconstruction reopened it on June 28, 2012.

places.name: Msgr. McGolrick Park
places.address: Russell St., Monitor St. bet. Nassau Ave. and Driggs Ave., Brooklyn
places.summary: A nine-acre neighborhood park with a landmarked 1910 shelter pavilion, a World War I memorial, a monument to the USS Monitor, a Sunday farmers' market, and a gated playground.
places.history: The City of Brooklyn acquired the land in 1889 and named it Winthrop Park for Assemblyman Winthrop Jones. A playground was created in 1897, and the shelter pavilion by the architectural firm of Helmle and Huberty was erected in 1910; it is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, recognized as a New York City landmark, and was restored in 1985 with a new roof, walkway repairs, a reconstructed colonnade, and replacement windows and doors. The park was renamed in 1941 for Monsignor Edward J. McGolrick, who served fifty years as pastor of St. Cecilia's Roman Catholic Church on Herbert Street.

places.name: WNYC Transmitter Park
places.address: West St. bet. Kent St. and Greenpoint Ave., Brooklyn
places.summary: Opened to the Greenpoint-Williamsburg communities in 2012 on the former working home of WNYC's radio transmission towers. It has a waterfront esplanade, an open lawn, a nautical-themed children's play area, and a recreational fishing pier at the end of Kent Street.

places.name: Bushwick Inlet Park
places.address: Kent Ave. bet. Quay St. and N 9 St., Brooklyn
places.summary: The centerpiece of the Greenpoint-Williamsburg waterfront, with a multipurpose athletic field, a green-roofed building, a viewing platform, a playground, and public waterfront access. A weekends-only pop-up section is open at 50 Kent Avenue.

places.name: Newtown Barge Playground
places.summary: A six-acre park with a playground, handball courts, and soccer fields, named for the barge canal terminal that once occupied the site. Parks acquired the land in 1942, and posted historical signage on site covers Greenpoint's founding.

places.name: Greenpoint Historic District
places.address: Roughly bounded by Kent, Calyer, Noble, and Franklin Streets, Clifford Place, and Manhattan Avenue, Brooklyn
places.summary: A 43-acre district of 363 buildings dating mostly from 1850 to 1900 — rowhouses, walk-ups, and commercial and religious buildings in Late Victorian and Italianate styles. It is a standing residential district, walkable from the sidewalk.
places.history: The Landmarks Preservation Commission designated the district on September 14, 1982 (Designation List 159, LP-1248). It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on September 26, 1983 under reference number 83001692.

places.name: Eberhard Faber Pencil Company Historic District
places.address: West Street between Greenpoint Avenue and Kent Street, Brooklyn
places.summary: The former pencil factory complex, viewable from the street; the buildings are not open to the public. Several of them now house the headquarters of Kickstarter.
places.history: Following a fire at the Manhattan plant in 1872, Faber moved the factory to Brooklyn, where it remained until 1956. Per the Landmarks Preservation Commission's designation report, the Faber company grew to become one of the largest pencil manufacturers in the world, with additional factories in Germany, Canada, and Argentina. The district was designated on October 30, 2007 (Designation List 397, LP-2264).

places.name: WORD Bookstore
places.summary: An independent bookstore on Franklin Street, part of the small WORD Brooklyn and Jersey City chain. It sells books and audiobooks and runs a membership program and book clubs.

places.name: Me and Paul's
places.summary: A dive bar serving Paulie Gee's wood-fired, Neapolitan-style pizza, open daily into the early morning. Walk-ins only. The pizzeria's own Greenpoint page now presents this address under the Me and Paul's name rather than the original Paulie Gee's branding.

entries.name: Msgr. McGolrick Park
entries.note: The 1910 shelter pavilion, the World War I memorial and the Monitor monument sit within a few paths of each other. A farmers' market runs on Sundays.

entries.name: Greenpoint Historic District
entries.note: Forty-three acres of rowhouses and walk-ups built between 1850 and 1900, best seen from the sidewalks around Kent, Calyer, Noble and Franklin Streets.

entries.name: WNYC Transmitter Park
entries.note: The waterfront esplanade runs to a recreational fishing pier at the end of Kent Street, on ground that once held WNYC's radio towers.

entries.name: Eberhard Faber Pencil Company Historic District
entries.note: The pencil works ran here from 1872 to 1956. The buildings are private — Kickstarter occupies several — so this one is looked at from West Street.

entries.name: McCarren Park
entries.note: Thirty-five acres of ballfields, courts and track shared with Williamsburg, plus the WPA-era pool that reopened in 2012 after a long closure.

entries.name: Bushwick Inlet Park
entries.note: A viewing platform, an athletic field and public waterfront access on Kent Avenue, with a weekends-only pop-up section at 50 Kent Avenue.

entries.name: Newtown Barge Playground
entries.note: Named for the barge canal terminal that stood here. Posted Parks signage on site tells the story of Greenpoint's Dutch founding.

entries.name: WORD Bookstore
entries.note: An independent shop on Franklin Street with book clubs and a membership program.

entries.name: Me and Paul's
entries.note: Wood-fired Neapolitan pizza from the Paulie Gee's kitchen, served in a dive bar on Greenpoint Avenue. Walk-ins only.

links.note: McCarren Park straddles the Williamsburg/Greenpoint border, and NYC Parks describes it as shared by both neighborhoods.
Greenpoint and East Williamsburg are both in Brooklyn Community District 1.
The cities of Brooklyn, Williamsburgh and Bushwick — which then included Greenpoint — merged in 1854.
